title: India Is Now Buying Oil from Four Continents. The Old Supply Chain Is Gone.
excerpt: Venezuela, Brazil, Angola, Nigeria, and Russia are filling the gap left by the Hormuz shutdown. What started as emergency procurement is becoming a permanent shift in how the world's third-largest oil importer sources its energy.
body:
India is no longer buying oil the way it did six months ago. The country's crude supply chain — once anchored in the Middle East with a heavy Russian supplement — has been pulled apart by the Strait of Hormuz crisis and rebuilt across four continents in real time.

Indian refiners raised imports from Venezuela, Brazil, Angola, and Nigeria in April and May to cover shortfalls caused by the ongoing disruption in Hormuz, according to preliminary Kpler data. At the same time, India is receiving about 1.9 million barrels per day of Russian oil and roughly 41,000 bpd from Iraq. The result is an oil basket that looks nothing like it did at the start of the year.

Venezuela has emerged as the most striking addition. The South American producer is on track to become India's fourth-largest crude supplier in May, reflecting stronger demand for heavy crude as Gulf flows remain constrained. Union Minister for Petroleum Hardeep Singh Puri told Venezuelan Interim President Delcy Rodriguez that Indian companies are willing to expand their participation in Venezuela's oil and gas industry. Rodriguez's visit to India focused on attracting long-term investment rather than relying on spot purchases — a signal that both sides see this as more than a temporary fix.

## The Hormuz Problem Has Not Gone Away

One hundred days into the conflict between the United States and Iran, the Strait of Hormuz remains effectively closed to normal commercial traffic. The latest escalation came over the weekend: US forces shot down six Iranian drones in 48 hours and struck radar installations on Goruk and Qeshm Island. Iran retaliated by firing missiles at US facilities in Kuwait and Bahrain.

Saudi Arabia and the UAE have increased shipments through pipelines that bypass the strait, and US crude exports have risen to records. But the alternatives cannot match the volume that once flowed through Hormuz. India receives about 40 percent of its oil imports from the Middle East through the waterway, and its commercial and strategic reserves cover only about 25 days of demand.

Brent crude settled at $93.09 a barrel on Friday. JPMorgan predicts Hormuz will reopen in June and expects Brent to remain near $100 for most of the year. If the strait stays closed, each additional month would add roughly $5 a barrel to the bank's third-quarter forecast and $15 to its fourth-quarter estimate.

## From Emergency Procurement to Structural Shift

What started as crisis buying is beginning to look like a permanent redrawing of India's energy map. The government and refiners have emphasised diversification to reduce exposure to supply shocks from the Hormuz chokepoint. State refiners Indian Oil, Bharat Petroleum, Hindustan Petroleum, and Mangalore Refinery and Petrochemicals have all been active in sourcing alternative cargoes.

The shift has geopolitical dimensions. India became the world's largest buyer of Russian seaborne crude after Moscow's 2022 Ukraine invasion, but it scaled back under US pressure — particularly after a trade deal that rolled back punitive tariffs. In February, India loaded just over 1 million barrels per day from Russia, roughly half of peak levels. The Hormuz crisis reversed that trajectory. India approached Washington seeking approval to resume Russian crude purchases because of the Iran conflict, and Russian oil sitting in Asian waters began moving again.

Brazil and West African producers are filling the gaps that neither Russia nor Venezuela can cover alone. Angola and Nigeria have seen increased demand from Indian refiners who need heavy and medium crudes that match the profiles their facilities were built to process.

## What This Means for NRIs

For the Indian diaspora watching from the US, UK, and Canada, the oil diversification story is not just about crude prices. India's energy costs ripple through everything from airline ticket prices to inflation in the cities their families live in. A sustained $90-plus oil price hits household budgets across India — from cooking gas to transport — and constrains the government's fiscal space for the subsidies and infrastructure spending that drive economic growth.

The old supply chain — Gulf crude through Hormuz, supplemented by Russian discounts — is gone. What replaces it will determine India's energy security for years to come.
